abstract: Data provenance, the origin and derivation history of data, is commonly used for security auditing, forensics and data analysis. While provenance loggers provide evidence of data changes, the integrity of the provenance logs is also critical for the integrity of the forensics process. abstract: The rapid integration of AI into IoT systems has outpaced the ability to explain and audit automated decisions, resulting in a serious transparency gap. We address this challenge by proposing a blockchain-based framework to create immutable audit trails of AI-driven IoT decisions. In our approach, each AI inference comprising key inputs, model ID, and output is logged to a permissioned blockchain ledger, ensuring that every decision is traceable and auditable. IoT devices and edge gateways submit cryptographically signed decision records via smart contracts, resulting in an immutable, timestamped log that is tamper-resistant. This decentralized approach guarantees non-repudiation and data integrity while balancing transparency with privacy (e.g., hashing personal data on-chain) to meet data protection norms. Our design aligns with emerging regulations, such as the EU AI Act’s logging mandate and GDPR’s transparency requirements. title: VERITAS OS: A Cryptographically Auditable, Safety-Aligned Decision Operating System for LLM-based Proto-AGI Agents
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: VERITAS OS is a Proto-AGI Decision Operating System designed to transform large language models (LLMs) into transparent, safety-aligned, and cryptographically auditable autonomous agents. Existing agent frameworks such as ReAct, AutoGPT, LangGraph, and DSPy provide iterative reasoning and tool use, but they lack the critical components required for high-stakes or regulated environments—namely structured safety gates, reproducible decision pipelines, persistent memory, world-state tracking, and tamper-evident audit logs. title: Votebox: a tamper-evident, verifiable voting machine
abstract:
This thesis details the design and implementation of V OTEBOX, a new software platform for building and evaluating secure and reliable electronic voting machines. Current electronic voting systems have experienced many high-profile software, hardware, and usability failures in real elections. Recent research has revealed systemic flaws in commercial voting systems that can cause malfunctions, lose votes, and possibly even allow outsiders to influence the outcome of a national election. These failures and flaws cast doubt on the accuracy of elections conducted with electronic systems and threaten to undermine public trust in the electoral system. 
While some consequently argue for total abandonment of electronic voting, VOTEBOX shows how a combination of security, distributed systems, and cryptographic principles can yield trustworthy and usable voting systems. It employs a pre-rendered user interface to reduce the size of the runtime system that must be absolutely trusted. title: VULCON
venue: ACM Transactions on Privacy and Security
abstract: Vulnerability remediation is a critical task in operational software and network security management. In this article, an effective vulnerability management strategy, called VULCON (VULnerability CONtrol), is developed and evaluated. The strategy is based on two fundamental performance metrics: (1) time-to-vulnerability remediation (TVR) and (2) total vulnerability exposure (TVE). VULCON takes as input real vulnerability scan reports, metadata about the discovered vulnerabilities, asset criticality, and personnel resources. VULCON uses a mixed-integer multiobjective optimization algorithm to prioritize vulnerabilities for patching, such that the above performance metrics are optimized subject to the given resource constraints. VULCON has been tested on multiple months of real scan data from a cyber-security operations center (CSOC). Results indicate an overall TVE reduction of 8.97% when VULCON optimizes a realistic security analyst workforce’s effort. Additionally, VULCON demonstrates that it can determine monthly resources required to maintain a target TVE score. As such, VULCON provides valuable operational guidance for improving vulnerability response processes in CSOCs.

title: Wazuh Alert Manager: An OpenSearch plugin for alert and case management in Wazuh-based Security Operations Centers
abstract: Security analysts using Wazuh for security monitoring typically report experiencing high alert volumes. However, in the Wazuh 4.12-4.14 dashboards considered in this paper, there is no native way to manage the alert lifecycle, analyst workload, handle independent multi-alert cases, or automate alert workflows. As a result, many SOCs running Wazuh add external case management tools like TheHive and DFIR-IRIS, increasing the technology stack and operational complexity. In this paper, we present the Wazuh Alert Manager plugin v2.0.2, built for Wazuh dashboard versions 4.12-4.14, to provide alert and case management, alert workflow automation, and reporting within the Wazuh dashboard. The plugin writes only to its indexes and only performs reads from Wazuh native alert indexes. In three benchmarking tests, the plugin processed 100,000 alerts on a standard all-in-one Wazuh VM with a median time of 238.081 seconds, resulting in exactly 42 cases, 5,000 alert auto-closures, 2,500 auto-assignments, and no actions on 87,200 benign alerts. The plugin is licensed under Apache 2.0 and archived on Zenodo.

title: Where to Go from Here
abstract: Security operations is a mindset. Healthcare entities do not necessarily need to have a dedicated security operations center or contract with a managed service provider delivering virtual security operations center (SOC) services. But the mindset needs to be there. Once the overarching cybersecurity program is designed and implemented, the real work on implementing security begins. In the forward to Snort: IDS and IPS Toolkit , Stephen Northcutt talks about the difference between managing security via checklists and policies and understanding how to implement security. This means frameworks like the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) are great tools to guide entities in implementing security, risk assessment, and management strategies – but more is needed. Entities must perform threat assessments and in-depth analysis of vulnerabilities and attack vectors to implement high-functioning detection capabilities. title: ПРОБЛЕМЫ ВНЕДРЕНИЯ ЦИФРОВЫХ ТЕХНОЛОГИЙ REGTECH И SUPTECH В ФИНАНСОВУЮ СФЕРУ
abstract:
В статье исследуются проблемы внедрения решений SupTech и RegTech в России. Основное внимание уделяется особенностям интеграции этих технологий в деятельность Центрального банка Российской Федерации. Цель исследования заключается в анализе ключевых характеристик и модельных рисков, связанных с применением SupTech и RegTech, а также в выявлении барьеров и возможностей для их успешного внедрения в российскую финансовую систему.
                  We look at the problems of implementing SupTech and RegTech solutions in Russia. The main focus is on the specific features of integrating these technologies into the activities of the Central Bank of the Russian Federation. The study is aimed at analyzing the key characteristics and model risks connected with the use of SupTech and RegTech as well as identifying barriers and opportunities for their successful implementation in the Russian financial system.
